judgment.summary: The four replacement paragraphs are factually accurate against the supplied source evidence, correctly scoped, clearly connected to their surrounding sections, and end in a usable work consequence. Paragraph 1 states that pattern learning and verbatim memorisation coexist; paragraph 2 reports the 2021 GPT-2 extraction study within its actual scope and explicitly refuses both the every-model generalisation and the model-as-archive misreading; paragraph 3 converts this into a concrete verification habit (open the original before attributing exact words); paragraph 4 in 5.4 repairs the numbers-not-articles claim so it no longer implies memorisation is impossible, with a correct cross-reference to 5.1. The voice is plain and conversational without banned template patterns, and no era joke or new analogy is needed — the plain mechanic carries the teaching. No material problem remains within the narrow correction scope. This is not publication approval and not whole-book approval.
unchangedContextConcerns: The 5.4 parameter table states GPT-4 at "~1.8 trillion (estimated)" parameters; OpenAI has never disclosed this figure, and presenting a leaked/unofficial estimate in a factual table could mislead readers even with the "(estimated)" hedge.

The same table names "Current frontier (2026): GPT-5.6, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.5" with "estimated 2T+" parameters — unverifiable, staleness-prone specifics of the kind the book's own currency guidance says to avoid or date-stamp in prose, not enshrine in an evergreen table.

5.1's boxed note claims that copying all the weights "would produce the same results" — for generative models with sampled output this is only true under deterministic settings; a beginner may over-conclude that identical weights guarantee identical answers.

5.1's "You can't point to one weight and say 'that's where it learned grammar'" is a reasonable beginner simplification but stated absolutely; it slightly overstates the opacity of trained models. Minor.
These concerns are outside the four corrected paragraphs; noting them does not constitute review or approval of the rest of the book.

claimChecks.sourceExcerpt: We demonstrate our attack on GPT-2, a language model trained on scrapes of the public Internet, and are able to extract hundreds of verbatim text sequences from the model's training data.
claimChecks.assessment: Supported. Model, method (querying), quantity ("hundreds"), and verbatim nature all match the publisher abstract; "queried" is supported by "recover individual training examples by querying the language model."

claimChecks.candidateExcerpt: That is evidence of memorisation in that model, not proof that every model remembers every article. It also does not turn a model into a dependable archive where you can look up any document it encountered.
claimChecks.sourceExcerpt: Scope limits: "Historical GPT-2 finding; not a claim about every contemporary product"; "Demonstrates that memorisation is possible; not that every training document is recoverable"
claimChecks.assessment: Supported scoping. The replacement's hedges map directly onto the source's stated scope limits and correctly separate demonstrated memorisation from reliable document lookup.

claimChecks.candidateExcerpt: an answer that sounds like a quotation is not proof of its source. If you need someone's exact words for a work document, open the original and compare the passage before you attribute it.

claimChecks.assessment: Consistent. The replacement draws only a verification-habit consequence and preserves the distinction between possible memorisation, reliable lookup, and authenticated quotation provenance without any provenance overclaim.

judgment.explainBack: AI-simulated explain-back (this is a model paraphrase, not evidence of human reader comprehension): \"A trained model is a huge pile of tuned numbers, and mostly those numbers encode patterns, like how sentences tend to go. But the same numbers can also store some exact passages from the training data — one 2021 study got GPT-2 to spit out hundreds of word-for-word chunks of its training text. That doesn't mean a model is a library where you can look anything up, and it doesn't mean every model memorised every article. It just means 'it learned patterns' and 'it can repeat a source' are both true at once. So if the model gives me something that reads like an exact quote, that's not proof of where it came from — before I put someone's exact words in a work document, I find the original and compare.\"
judgment.transfer: New transfer example: you ask a chatbot for the exact wording of a clause from a well-known standard contract template, and it produces text formatted like a quotation, complete with a section number. The corrected teaching says three different things could be happening: the model may have genuinely memorised that clause from training data, it may be generating plausible clause-shaped language, or a lookup tool may (or may not) have actually retrieved the current template. Confident quotation formatting distinguishes none of these. Before pasting that clause into an agreement, you open the current official template and compare word for word — because memorisation is possible, reliable lookup is not guaranteed, and quotation-sounding output is not provenance.
limitations: Source verification was limited to the publisher and arXiv abstracts plus the stated scope limits; the full Carlini et al. paper was not inspected, so claims were checked only against abstract-level evidence.
The vendor training excerpt is bounded; per its instructions, no stronger vendor claims about memorisation, privacy, or legal compliance were used or assessed.
The explain-back above is AI-simulated and is not evidence that human readers understand the correction.
